content: Ovarian cancer is the sixth most common cancer affecting women globally. The most prevalent type is epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC), and approximately 75% of women are diagnosed at an advanced stage (stage III or IV), where the disease has already spread beyond the pelvis. Standard treatment involves a combination of surgery and platinum-based chemotherapy. While initial responses to chemotherapy are often favorable, the majority of women with advanced disease experience relapse. Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) are a class of anticancer agents that function by inhibiting the repair of DNA damage in cancer cells. This mechanism is particularly effective in patients with mutations in the breast cancer susceptibility genes (BRCA1 and BRCA2) or other defects in homologous recombination repair (HRD). PARPi represent a novel therapeutic approach distinct from conventional chemotherapy. The objective of this review was to evaluate the benefits and risks of PARPi in the treatment of epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC). Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were identified through comprehensive searches of multiple databases and trial registries. Studies were included if they compared PARPi to no treatment, PARPi to conventional chemotherapy, or PARPi in combination with chemotherapy versus chemotherapy alone. Outcomes assessed included overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), objective response rate (ORR), quality of life (QoL), and adverse events. Fifteen studies involving 6,109 participants were included. Four studies focused on newly diagnosed advanced EOC (3,070 participants), while 11 studies addressed recurrent EOC (3,039 participants). The majority of participants had BRCA mutations (either somatic or germline) or HRD in their tumors. The studies varied in their comparisons and were assessed for risk of bias, with eight studies judged to have a low risk of bias in most domains. However, QoL data were generally poorly reported. Newly Diagnosed Advanced EOC 1. PARPi with Chemotherapy vs. Chemotherapy Alone: Two studies (1,564 participants) showed that combining PARPi with chemotherapy may result in little to no difference in PFS (hazard ratio [HR] 0.82, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.49 to 1.38; very low-certainty evidence). At 12 months, 63% of patients receiving PARPi showed no disease progression compared to 69% in the placebo group. Severe adverse events (SevAE, grade 3 or higher) were slightly more frequent with PARPi (45%) compared to chemotherapy alone (51%) (risk ratio [RR] 1.13, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.20; high-certainty evidence). QoL was likely similar between the two groups (mean difference [MD] 1.56, 95% CI -0.42 to 3.54; moderate-certainty evidence). 2. PARPi Monotherapy as Maintenance vs. Placebo: Two studies (1,124 participants) suggested that PARPi probably results in little to no difference in OS (HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.13; moderate-certainty evidence). At 12 months, 68% of patients receiving PARPi were alive compared to 62% in the placebo group. PARPi may improve PFS (HR 0.42, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.92; low-certainty evidence). At 12 months, 55% of patients receiving PARPi showed no disease progression compared to 24% in the placebo group. There may be an increased risk of SevAE with PARPi (54%) compared to placebo (19%) (RR 2.87, 95% CI 1.65 to 4.99; very low-certainty evidence). QoL may be slightly reduced with PARPi, but the clinical significance of this reduction is uncertain (MD -3.00, 95% CI -4.48 to -1.52; moderate-certainty evidence). Recurrent Platinum-Sensitive EOC 1. PARPi Monotherapy vs. Chemotherapy: Two studies (331 participants) indicated that PARPi may result in little to no difference in OS (HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.47; low-certainty evidence). At 36 months, 18% of patients receiving PARPi were alive compared to 17% in the placebo group. Evidence on the effect of PARPi on PFS was very uncertain (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.38; very low-certainty evidence). At 12 months, 26% of patients receiving PARPi showed no disease progression compared to 22% in the placebo group. Rates of SevAE (grade 3 or higher) were similar between PARPi (50%) and chemotherapy (47%) (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.39; low-certainty evidence). 2. PARPi Maintenance Therapy vs. Placebo: Two studies (560 participants) suggested that PARPi may result in little to no difference in OS (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.20; moderate-certainty evidence). At 36 months, 21% of patients receiving PARPi were alive compared to 17% in the placebo group. PARPi maintenance therapy likely results in a significant improvement in PFS (HR 0.34, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.42; high-certainty evidence). At 12 months, 37% of patients receiving PARPi showed no disease progression compared to 5.5% in the placebo group. PARPi maintenance therapy may increase the risk of SevAE (51%) compared to placebo (19%) (RR 2.62, 95% CI 1.85 to 3.72; low-certainty evidence). QoL may be similar between the two groups (MD 1.20, 95% CI -1.75 to 4.16; low-certainty evidence). Recurrent Platinum-Resistant EOC 1. PARPi vs. Chemotherapy: Two studies provided very low-certainty evidence, making it difficult to draw conclusions about the effects of PARPi on OS, PFS, QoL, or adverse events in this population. Authors' Conclusions PARPi maintenance therapy after chemotherapy may improve PFS in women with newly diagnosed and recurrent platinum-sensitive EOC. However, there appears to be little to no effect on OS, although OS data remain immature. The use of PARPi is associated with an increased risk of SevAE. Unfortunately, data on QoL outcomes are limited, and further research is needed to clarify the role of PARPi in platinum-resistant disease.
